introduction-when-crds-arent-enough.core: CRDs store objects in etcd with standard CRUD semantics, validation and versioning, which is perfect for most extensions. But some APIs need custom storage (an external database), computed or ephemeral results (live metrics), special subresources, very high write volumes unsuitable for etcd, or non-standard verbs. The API aggregation layer lets you serve those from your own API server behind the main one.

first_principles.problem: A team stores high-frequency metrics as CRDs and overloads etcd.
truths: etcd isn't built for high-volume data.
Some data is computed, not stored.
derivation: Use **aggregation** for computed, external or high-volume data.

analogy.title: A department store with a concession counter
analogy.story: Most goods are on the store's own shelves; the concession runs its own stock system behind the store's front door.
analogy.breaks: Customers notice concessions; clients can't tell aggregated APIs from built-in ones.

example.title: Right tool per need
flow: Audit search over external store → aggregated API

check.q: When should you prefer API aggregation over CRDs?
check.a: When you need custom storage, computed/ephemeral data, high write volumes or non-standard semantics.

architecture-the-api-proxy.core: With aggregation, kube-apiserver acts as a proxy: requests for a registered group/version (e.g. /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1) are authenticated by kube-apiserver and forwarded over TLS to the extension API server's Service, along with identity headers. The extension server performs authorisation (via SubjectAccessReview), executes the request and returns a standard Kubernetes response.

first_principles.problem: Engineers wonder how kubectl top works without metrics being stored in etcd.
truths: The main API server can route by API group.
derivation: Extension server **trusts** front-proxy headers via CA.

analogy.title: A receptionist forwarding calls to a specialist department
analogy.story: The caller is verified at reception and the department handles the request.
analogy.breaks: Phone transfers are simple; proxying requires mutual TLS and trusted header configuration.

example.title: Request path
flow: Proxies to metrics-server Service with X-Remote-User

check.q: How does an extension API server learn who the caller is?
check.a: From front-proxy identity headers (e.g. X-Remote-User) set by kube-apiserver and trusted via a configured CA.

the-canonical-example-metrics-server.core: metrics-server scrapes resource usage from each kubelet's /metrics/resource endpoint, keeps the latest values in memory and serves them through the aggregated metrics.k8s.io API (NodeMetrics, PodMetrics). kubectl top, HPA and VPA consume it. It's not a monitoring system: no history, just current usage for autoscaling.

first_principles.problem: HPA reports 'unable to get metrics' and kubectl top fails.
derivation: Use **Prometheus** for history and custom metrics.

analogy.title: A live scoreboard, not a statistics archive
analogy.story: It shows the current score for decisions now, not last season's results.
analogy.breaks: Scoreboards are public; metrics.k8s.io access is RBAC-controlled.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Kubelet cert not trusted → add proper CA or --kubelet-preferred-address-types.

code.text:
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[0]}'
kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/metrics-server | tail
kubectl top nodes

check.a: No; it keeps only recent values in memory for autoscaling and kubectl top.

the-glue-apiservice-resource.core: An APIService object (apiregistration.k8s.io) registers a group and version, points to a Service (namespace, name, port), includes a caBundle to verify the extension server's TLS certificate, and sets groupPriorityMinimum and versionPriority for discovery ordering. Its Available condition reflects whether kube-apiserver can reach the backend.

first_principles.problem: kubectl commands hang or show discovery errors because an aggregated API is unavailable.

analogy.title: A directory listing for a concession counter
analogy.story: It says which products are sold there and how to verify the staff's ID.
analogy.breaks: Directory entries don't break the whole store; unavailable APIServices can slow or break discovery.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Restore adapter Pods or delete the stale APIService.

code.text:
kubectl get apiservices | grep -v True
# v1beta1.custom.metrics.k8s.io  monitoring/prometheus-adapter  False (MissingEndpoints)

check.q: What does the caBundle field in an APIService provide?
check.a: The CA used by kube-apiserver to verify the extension server's TLS certificate.

authentication-delegation-trusting-the-p.core: Extension API servers delegate auth: they trust requests proxied by kube-apiserver by validating its client certificate against the requestheader client CA and reading identity from X-Remote-User/X-Remote-Group headers. For authorisation they call back with SubjectAccessReview, and for direct client tokens they can use TokenReview. RBAC on the extension-apiserver-authentication ConfigMap and auth-delegator role enable this.

first_principles.problem: An extension API server accepts spoofed identity headers from any client inside the cluster.
truths: Headers can be forged unless the sender is verified.

analogy.title: Trusting a colleague's note only if it's on official letterhead
analogy.story: Anyone can write 'approved by Alice', but only reception's stamped letterhead is trusted.
analogy.breaks: Letterheads can be photocopied; mTLS certificates can't be forged without the private key.

check.q: How does an extension API server authorise requests?
check.a: By sending SubjectAccessReview requests to kube-apiserver, reusing cluster RBAC.

crd-vs-aggregation-layer-choosing-the-ri.core: Choose CRDs for most extensions: no server to run, etcd storage, schema validation, CEL rules, versioning and conversion webhooks, and full tooling support. Choose aggregation when you need custom storage backends, computed or read-only views, extreme scale beyond etcd, protobuf, custom subresources or verbs, and accept the cost of building, securing and operating an API server.

first_principles.problem: A team builds an aggregated API server for simple configuration objects and now maintains thousands of lines of code.
truths: Simpler solutions are easier to operate.

analogy.title: Using the store's shelves versus opening your own shop inside
analogy.story: Shelves are easy; your own shop gives control but you must staff and secure it.
analogy.breaks: Shops can be closed easily; removing an aggregated API affects all clients using it.

example.title: Decision checklist
flow: Is it config-like with CRUD? → CRD
Must data live outside etcd? → aggregation
Is it computed on read? → aggregation

check.q: Why are CRDs usually preferred over aggregated APIs?
check.a: They need no custom server, use etcd storage and get validation, versioning and tooling for free.
